At the gram panchayat office in Yavatmal district, Tejas slapped the yield register on the table. "Look. The six villages that got solar pumps last year harvested far more cotton. The pumps did it."
Vinita, the block's agriculture officer, turned the pages slowly. "Maybe. But which villages got pumps first?"
"The ones that applied fast."
"The ones whose sarpanches know the paperwork, where farmers already had some money. They might have done better anyway. Or did the farmers who were already doing well put in extra for the pumps?" She tapped the rainfall column. "And the eastern side got more rain this year. That's where most pumps are."
Tejas frowned. "So the pumps did nothing?"
"I didn't say that. Find me six similar villages without pumps, same rain, same size farms, and we compare. Then we'll know what to tell the collector."

qa.q: What does the yield register show, according to Tejas?
qa.a: The six villages that got solar pumps last year harvested far more cotton.

qa.q: What is Vinita thinking when she asks which villages got pumps first?
qa.a: Vinita feels doubtful about the claim, suspecting those villages were different to begin with, with better paperwork and more money, so their good harvest might not be the pumps' doing.

qa.q: What comparison does Vinita ask for, and why does it help?
qa.a: Six similar villages without pumps, with the same rain and farm size; comparing them separates the pumps' effect from rain and money.

qa.q: How might Tejas feel when Vinita questions the finding?
qa.a: Tejas might feel the good news is being brushed aside at first, though Vinita makes clear she isn't saying the pumps did nothing.

grounding: It shows an officer asking about third causes, reverse direction and rainfall, and asking for a comparison group before crediting the pumps.

"Customers with the loyalty app spend forty percent more," Kofi announced, pointing at the chart on the big screen in the Rotterdam office. "Let's push the app harder and watch sales climb."
Santiago leaned back. "Or the people who already spend a lot are exactly the ones who bother to download it. That runs the arrow the other way."
"Hm."
"And most of these downloads came in December. Everyone spends more in December." He scrolled. "Also, app users live closer to our shops. Distance could drive both."
Kofi crossed his arms. "So what would convince you?"
"Send the app invite to a random half of new customers next month, and not to the other half. If the invited half spend more, I'm on your side."
Kofi sighed, then grinned. "Fine. Random half it is."

qa.q: What figure did Kofi announce about app customers?
qa.a: Customers with the loyalty app spend forty percent more.

qa.q: Why does Santiago doubt that the app is what makes people spend more?
qa.a: He suspects big spenders are simply the ones who download it, that December inflated spending, and that living near the shops could drive both.

qa.q: What test does Santiago propose, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Invite a random half of new customers and not the other half; since chance decides who gets the invite, a spending gap would point to the app itself. 👍

qa.q: What would change if the invited half spent no more than the others?
qa.a: The team would learn the link came from who downloads the app, not from the app, and could stop spending effort pushing it.

grounding: It shows an analyst raising reverse direction, a third cause and timing coincidence, and proposing a random comparison group before claiming cause.

The monthly meeting at the women's hostel ran late, and Tenzin had one last slide. "Residents who come to morning yoga took far fewer sick days this term. I think we should make it compulsory."
Nirmala, the welfare officer, looked at the list of names. "Before we decide, can I ask a few things? Who comes to yoga at six? People who already sleep early and feel well. Someone with a cold isn't getting up for it. So feeling well might bring people to yoga, not only the other way round."
Tenzin nodded slowly.
"And the yoga group is mostly final-years with fewer late labs. That could matter too." She pulled up a blank sheet. "Could we compare residents with similar timetables, some who start yoga next month and some who don't, and look again at the end of term?"

qa.q: What did Tenzin want to make compulsory?
qa.a: Morning yoga.

qa.q: What is Nirmala thinking when she says someone with a cold isn't getting up for it?
qa.a: Nirmala feels doubtful about the slide, suspecting the link runs backwards: residents who already feel well are the ones who come, so fewer sick days might not be the yoga's doing.

qa.q: Why is Nirmala's suggested comparison better than deciding now?
qa.a: Comparing residents with similar timetables, some starting yoga and some not, removes the timetable and early-sleeper differences, so any gap is more likely due to yoga.

qa.q: How might residents feel if yoga became compulsory because of this slide?
qa.a: Some might resent being pulled out of bed at six for a benefit nobody has shown, especially those with late labs.

grounding: It shows an officer checking for reverse direction and a hidden third factor and proposing a fair comparison before making a rule.

Subject: Smart boards and results, before we send the funders' report

Hi Ira,
I know the draft says the smart boards "raised Class 8 scores by 14 marks". The link is real in the data. I'm just not ready to say the boards caused it, and I'd like one more week.
Three things are bothering me. First, the twelve schools that got boards are mostly in the ward with more teachers per class. That alone could explain better scores. Second, the direction: the district gave boards first to schools that were already doing well, as a reward. Third, it's one year of results, and one year can swing by chance.
What I'd like to do is compare them with the eight schools on the waiting list that look most like them, same ward, same teacher numbers, same scores two years ago. If the gap holds there, I'll sign the sentence happily.
Aadhya

qa.q: How many schools on the waiting list does Aadhya want to compare with?
qa.a: The eight schools on the waiting list that look most like the board schools.

qa.q: What is Aadhya worried about if the report goes out as drafted?
qa.a: Aadhya is worried the report will claim the boards caused the higher scores when more teachers, the district rewarding strong schools, or a lucky year could explain the link.

qa.q: Which step in Aadhya's plan is the strongest, and why?
qa.a: Comparing with the most similar waiting-list schools, because it shows what scores looked like without boards, so any gap left is more likely due to the boards.

qa.q: How might Ira feel reading this email just before the funders' report?
qa.a: Ira may feel a bit frustrated by the delay but also relieved that a claim the funders might check has been tested before it goes out.

grounding: It shows a careful analyst asking whether a third cause, reverse direction or chance explains a link, and seeking a comparison group before claiming cause.

Jyoti, you asked on the show what I actually do at the academy. Okay, here's one story.
Last season the head coach showed me a chart. Players who did the new video sessions improved their batting average far more than players who didn't. He wanted to make them compulsory and buy three more cameras.
I'm the analyst, so my first question was, who chose which players went to the video sessions? Turns out the coaches picked the ones they thought were "about to break through". So the players were already rising. That's the direction problem.
Then I asked what else those players had. Extra net time, as it happened. Third cause.
So we ran it properly. Next term, among players the coaches rated the same, half got video sessions by draw and half didn't. The video group did improve, a little. Much less than the chart. We bought one camera, not three.
Ankita, analyst. That's the job.

qa.q: How many cameras did the academy finally buy?
qa.a: One camera, not three.

qa.q: How did Ankita feel about the head coach's chart at first, and why?
qa.a: Ankita was sceptical, suspecting the chart looked better than the truth because coaches had picked players who were already rising and those players also had extra net time.

qa.q: Which choice made Ankita's approach convincing, and why?
qa.a: Splitting similarly rated players by draw into video and no-video groups; it removed the coaches' choices and the extra net time as explanations, so the small real effect could be seen.

qa.q: How might the head coach have felt when the proper test showed a much smaller gain?
qa.a: The head coach might have been disappointed after hoping for a big win, but also better placed to spend money on what actually helps players.

grounding: It shows a careful analyst checking reverse direction and a third cause, then using a fair comparison group before claiming the video sessions helped.

passage: I sat next to Sachin in the Friday review, so I saw it up close. Our regional head put up a chart: the eight cafés that got the new playlist in spring sold more cold drinks than the rest. "Roll it out everywhere," the head said. Sachin tapped his pen twice, the way he does before disagreeing. "Which cafés got it first?" The newest ones, in the big malls. "Then the mall crowds might explain both," he said. "And spring is when cold drinks go up anyway. Can we compare with mall cafés that didn't get the playlist?" The room went quiet. I couldn't tell if he was nervous; his voice stayed level. Two weeks later the comparison came back: almost no difference. I'm Jyoti, and I've copied his pen-tapping ever since.

qa.q: Which cafés got the new playlist first?
qa.a: The newest ones, in the big malls, got it first.

qa.q: What do Sachin's pen-tapping and level voice suggest about his state of mind?
qa.a: They suggest he was uneasy with the quick conclusion and determined to check it, though Jyoti couldn't tell whether he felt nervous.

qa.q: Which of Sachin's questions did the most useful work, and why?
qa.a: Asking to compare with mall cafés that didn't get the playlist, because that comparison group separates the playlist from the crowds and the season.

qa.q: How might the regional head have felt when the comparison came back?
qa.a: The head might have felt a little embarrassed, but also relieved not to roll out a change that made almost no difference.

grounding: Shows an analyst asking whether a third cause or the season explains a sales link and asking for a comparison group before claiming cause.

Monday. Kavitha burst into the NGO office with a spreadsheet. "The children in our evening reading club improved twice as much as the others this term!" Salma, the programme analyst, read it slowly. "Who chose to join?" "Well, the keen ones. Their parents signed them up." Salma wrote three words on a sticky note: keen, parents, luck.
The next Thursday. Salma found the waiting list: forty children whose parents had also signed up but for whom there had been no space. "They're our comparison," she told Kavitha. "Same keen families, no club yet."
Three weeks later. The new numbers came in. The club children still improved more than the waiting list, but by far less than the first chart had suggested. Kavitha sighed, then smiled. "Smaller, but real." Salma pinned the sticky note above her desk.

qa.q: What did Salma use as a comparison group?
qa.a: She used the waiting list: forty children whose parents had also signed up but for whom there had been no space.

qa.q: Why did Salma write 'keen, parents, luck' on a sticky note?
qa.a: Salma felt cautious rather than excited; she suspected that keen children, involved parents or plain luck could explain the gain, not only the club.

qa.q: Why was the waiting list a smart comparison?
qa.a: Those children came from equally keen families, so any extra gain in the club group is more likely due to the club itself.

qa.q: How did Kavitha's feelings change from Monday to the final numbers?
qa.a: Kavitha went from bursting with excitement to a small sigh, then accepted a smaller but real effect with a smile.

grounding: Shows an analyst asking whether keen families or luck explain a link and finding a comparison group before claiming the club caused the gain.

passage: Samir, sit, you'll like this one. I, Yogesh, was about your age, twenty-four, in my first year at the district agriculture office. My boss dropped a report on my desk: villages with more tractors had bigger harvests. The plan was to send tractors to every village. I was new and scared to speak. But I kept thinking: which villages have tractors? The ones with canal water. Maybe water grows the crops and also makes farmers rich enough to buy tractors. And maybe good harvests bought the tractors, not the other way round. So I asked for two lists: canal villages with few tractors, and dry villages with many. My boss grumbled for a week. The lists showed water did most of the work. The funds went to repairing canals instead. Always ask what else could explain it, beta.

qa.q: What did the report on young Yogesh's desk claim?
qa.a: It claimed that villages with more tractors had bigger harvests.

qa.q: What was young Yogesh feeling when the report arrived, and what kept the doubt alive?
qa.a: Yogesh felt new and scared to speak, but a nagging curiosity about canal water, and about which came first, kept the doubt going.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Asking for canal villages with few tractors and dry villages with many; those comparison lists showed water did most of the work, so the funds went to canals.

qa.q: How might the boss have felt about the request for two more lists?
qa.a: The boss seems to have been irritated by the delay, grumbling for a week, before the lists changed the plan.

grounding: Shows a young analyst asking whether water, reverse direction or coincidence explained a tractors-and-harvests link and comparing villages first.

passage: The regional manager wanted the answer by six: should every store in the chain start playing music? Pallavi, the analyst, had the data by four. Stores with music sold more, clearly. Her colleague Kishore was already drafting the email. "It's obvious. Music causes sales." Pallavi held up a hand. The office printer was jammed and the air conditioning had died; she had less than two hours. But she made herself ask three questions. Could something else cause both? She checked: the stores with music were mostly the big ones in malls, with more customers anyway. Could it run backwards? Busier stores might simply be the ones whose managers bothered with music. Was there a fair comparison? She found six mall stores that had started music only last month, and six similar ones that hadn't. Sales in both groups moved the same. At 5:50 she wrote: "No clear effect yet. Suggest a proper trial."

qa.q: How many mall stores had started music only last month?
qa.a: Six mall stores.

qa.q: What was Pallavi feeling when Kishore called it obvious?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and careful, not wanting to claim a cause under time pressure without checking other explanations.

qa.q: Which steps made Pallavi's answer trustworthy?
qa.a: Asking whether a third cause or reverse direction could explain the link, and comparing similar stores with and without music before deciding.

qa.q: How might the regional manager see Pallavi's email?
qa.a: The manager might feel a little disappointed at no quick answer, but gets a safer recommendation for a proper trial.

grounding: Shows a careful analyst, under time pressure, checking for a third cause, reversed direction and a comparison group before claiming music causes sales.

Last quarter my manager, Darshan, walked into our bay grinning. "Customers who use the new help chat spend thirty percent more. Put it in the board deck: chat drives sales."
I'm Parul, and I've learned to be the annoying one in these moments. I asked three questions out loud. Could a third thing cause both? People buying expensive fridges ask more questions and also spend more. Could it run backwards? Maybe spending more makes you need help, not the other way round. Could it be a fluke of one festive month?
Darshan sighed. "So what do you want?"
"A comparison group. Show the chat button to half the visitors at random for four weeks, and hide it from the other half."
We did. The gap shrank to three percent. Real, but small.
The board deck said three. Darshan grumbled, then thanked me in the meeting.

qa.q: How much more did chat users spend, according to Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan said customers who used the new help chat spent thirty percent more.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when Darshan wanted to claim that chat drives sales?
qa.a: Parul felt cautious and a little uneasy, wary that a third cause, reversed direction or a festive fluke could explain the link.

qa.q: Why was the comparison group the right next step?
qa.a: Showing the chat to a random half of visitors separated the chat's real effect from big spenders asking more questions, and revealed only a small gap.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when the gap shrank to three percent?
qa.a: Darshan was probably disappointed and a bit grumpy at losing the big claim, but grateful enough to thank Parul in the meeting.

grounding: Shows a careful analyst asking about third causes, reverse direction and coincidence, and using a comparison group before claiming cause.

passage:
Supervisor's note, public health data unit. Written by Mohit, team lead.
This week Yogesh, our newest analyst, was asked to confirm a link for a district report: villages with more mobile phone towers had more reported fever cases.
Several people in the office had already decided the towers were the cause. Yogesh didn't argue. He listed other possibilities on the whiteboard: bigger villages get more towers and also have more clinics that report fever; more towers could mean better roads, so more people reach a clinic; and the data came from one monsoon season.
Then he asked for a comparison: villages of the same size, with and without new towers, over three years. Once size was matched, the link almost vanished.
What I did next: I asked Yogesh to present his whiteboard to the whole unit on Friday, and added his three questions to our report checklist.

qa.q: What link was Yogesh asked to confirm?
qa.a: That villages with more mobile phone towers had more reported fever cases.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh stay calm when others had decided the towers were the cause?
qa.a: Yogesh felt curious rather than alarmed, and was careful to check whether village size, roads or one monsoon season explained the link.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's comparison fair?
qa.a: Matching villages of the same size, with and without new towers, over three years removed the size effect, and the link almost vanished.

qa.q: How did Mohit see Yogesh's work?
qa.a: Mohit was impressed enough to ask Yogesh to present on Friday and to add the three questions to the report checklist.

grounding: Shows a careful young analyst asking about third causes and one-season coincidence and finding a comparison group before claiming cause.

Tuesday.
Shalini ma'am announced today that front-row students score higher, so from Monday the weakest kids move to the front. Everyone clapped.
I didn't. I kept thinking. Who chooses the front row? The keen kids, the ones whose parents push them, the ones who can see the board. So maybe keenness causes both the seat and the marks. Or maybe it runs backwards: kids who do well feel confident sitting up front. Or maybe it's just this one batch.
After the meeting I asked her if we could try it properly: move seats by lottery in two sections for a term, keep the other two as they are, and compare. She laughed and said I sound like a scientist, but agreed to try it in Class 7.
It might still help. I just want to know it helps before we tell parents it does.
Bhupen

qa.a: Shalini ma'am announced that front-row students score higher, so the weakest kids will move to the front from Monday.

qa.q: Why didn't Bhupen clap?
qa.a: Bhupen felt doubtful and uneasy, thinking keenness, confidence or one batch could explain the link rather than the seats themselves.

qa.q: What test does Bhupen propose, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Moving seats by lottery in two sections for a term and comparing them with two unchanged sections gives a comparison group before claiming cause.

qa.q: How does Shalini ma'am react to the idea?
qa.a: Shalini ma'am is amused and calls Bhupen a scientist, but is open enough to agree to a trial in Class 7.
